This notebook provides exercises on correlations and t-tests: computing them, reporting the results with the `report` package, and turning them into tables with the `broom` package so that they can be computed group by group with the tidyverse.
The data used here comes from the ISLR package that you will need to install first.





```{r}
# load packages
library(tidyverse)
library(ISLR)
library(report)
```




```{r}
data(Wage)
head(Wage)
```

## The "report" package

Sometimes it might be tricky to accurately report the results of an analysis. The `report` package can help!

```{r}
cor_result <- cor.test(Wage$wage, Wage$age)
report(cor_result)

```


It works with many statistical tests. Try it on the t-test that was computed earlier.

**Hint:** if you wrote the t-test with a formula and `data = Wage` (for example `t_test_result <- t.test(wage ~ health, data = Wage)`), give the data to `report()` as well: `report(t_test_result, data = Wage)`. Otherwise `report()` can only approximate the effect size (Cohen's d) and prints a warning.


```{r}

```


## The "broom" package

```{r}
library(broom)
```


```{r}

t_test_result <- t.test(Wage$wage~Wage$health)
broom::tidy(t_test_result)

```



## Compute stats the tidyverse way

`summarise()` can store a `broom::tidy()` result when that result has a single
row, as it does for a t-test or a correlation test (dplyr 1.1 or later). Use
`reframe()` when the result can have several rows; it also works with
`group_by()`.

```{r}
# t.test via reframe — works on the whole dataset
Wage |>
  reframe(broom::tidy(t.test(wage ~ health)))
```

```{r}
# cor.test via reframe
Wage |>
  reframe(broom::tidy(cor.test(wage, year)))
```




What's great about this approach is that we can now use the power of tidyverse. 

For example, imagine we want to compute a t-test of wage for two levels of health (as above) but separately for each level of education. 

In base R, this would involve quite a lot of coding; with the tidyverse and broom, this becomes a breeze.
